name: PT Cisarua Mountain Dairy Tbk

frontmatter.title: Cimory: the dairy franchise is intact, the margin is the question
frontmatter.summary: Cimory has delivered its fastest volume-led sales growth in years while operating profit barely moved: input costs and the rupiah took the difference. We initiate with ADD and a twelve-month target of Rp4,975, a 22.1% total return, on a business that is net cash, reinvests 7.0% of sales and earns a 30.7% return on equity.
thesis: Demand is not the problem. Net sales rose to 9,930 IDR bn in the first nine months of 2026, led by Premium Dairy at 4,372 IDR bn, described by management as volume-led growth across every product category [S7].

Margins are the problem. Gross margin fell to 42.9% from the 45.3% of FY2025 as whole milk powder, beef and the rupiah lifted input costs, and operating profit grew only to 1,860 IDR bn against the prior year period [S7][S2].
The balance sheet funds the growth. Net debt of -1,203.3 - a net cash position - against 2,733.2 of EBITDA, and capex of 942.5 is covered by operating cash flow [S7].

The stock trades at 15.5x FY2026E earnings and 11.9x EV/EBITDA for a business earning 30.7% on equity; the primary DCF of Rp4,708 is above the Rp4,250 price, so the ADD rests on the cash-flow method rather than on a re-rating of the multiple [S0].
Control is concentrated: insiders hold 80.7%, the free float is 18.6%, and the Sutantio family sets strategy through the founder-chairmanship [S6].

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results and the final dividend; the margin line is the event, not the sales line
Q4 2026 input-cost update: whole milk powder and beef purchase prices for the new contract window
Annual general meeting and declaration of the FY2026 final dividend against the interim already paid

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Cisarua Mountain Dairy (Cimory) with a ADD rating and a twelve-month target of Rp4,975, against a last price of Rp4,250: 17.1% of price upside and 22.1% of total return once the dividend is counted. The target is our blended value of Rp4,655 rolled forward one year at the 11.0% cost of equity and net of the dividend paid along the way. The primary method does the work: the discounted cash flow alone is worth Rp4,708, above the share price, and the two multiple cross-checks sit below it. That ordering matters. The recommendation is not a bet that Cimory re-rates to its old multiple; it is a cash-flow claim that volume-led growth, a partial margin recovery and a business that needs no external capital are worth more than the market pays today, with the downside bounded by a net-cash balance sheet.

This is the revision after the second review round, and the change is the discount rate rather than an operating assumption. The Sector Lead is right that the 0.70 beta build alone gives a cost of equity below the floor of the house compounder card's mandated IDR band, and that the previous draft presented that sub-band number as if it were the pinned build. We now add the company premium of 0.5% that the house already applies to ADES.JK for the same small-float, single-controller register, which puts the cost of equity and the WACC at 11.0%, the band floor [S0]. At that rate the blended value is Rp4,655, the twelve-month target Rp4,975 and the total return 22.1%, which on the house thresholds is a ADD rather than a BUY. No operating assumption was changed to protect the call: the target is lower only because the discount rate is higher, and the DCF itself remains above the share price.

The rest of the revision stands from the first round. The beta is the house consumer-staples default of 0.70; we previously used a higher figure with no source, and the lower one is worth roughly a seventh of the DCF. The agricultural-deck cost links are zeroed, because the engine applies the deck's one-year forecast as a permanent penalty and the linked commodities are marginal to Cimory's cost base [S7]. The dividend payout is set to the 78.0% the company has actually paid in each of the last two years, not a lower figure we could not source [S7]. And capex and working capital are now taken from the 30 September 2026 accounts rather than from an annualised guess: capex of 423 IDR bn of fixed assets plus 268 IDR bn of advances plus 19.5 IDR bn of right-of-use additions, and operating working capital of 3,832 IDR bn of current assets less 341 IDR bn of cash and 558 IDR bn of marketable securities, less 1,924 IDR bn of current liabilities [S5].

The investment debate is not about demand. In the first nine months of 2026 Cimory grew net sales to 9,930 IDR bn, with Premium Dairy at 4,372 IDR bn against 4,075 IDR bn for the whole of FY2025 and Premium Consumer Foods at 5,557 IDR bn [S7]. Management describes five consecutive quarters of strong double-digit dairy growth driven by volume, across all product categories, supported by outlet expansion to 236,364 outlets and 11,274 agents [S7]. That is about as clean a volume story as an Indonesian staples company has produced this cycle.

The debate is about what the volume cost. Gross profit rose only to 4,260 IDR bn in the same nine months while operating profit reached 1,860 IDR bn, and net profit 1,710 IDR bn, because whole milk powder at US$5,615/tonne and beef at US$3,987/tonne sit well above their FY2024 levels of US$4,562/tonne and US$3,890/tonne, and a weaker rupiah made every imported tonne dearer [S7]. The company carries six months of milk-powder and raw-beef supply purchased in advance and still could not hold the margin [S7]. Gross margin fell from 45.3% in FY2025 to 42.9% in our FY2026 estimate, and because the company kept investing in brand and distribution - selling and marketing spend rose faster than sales - operating margin fell to 18.4% from 21.1% [S7].

Our variant view is that both legs of that squeeze are cyclical rather than structural, but only partially reversible within the forecast window. We model gross margin recovering to 43.9% by FY2030 - still below the FY2025 peak - and operating margin to 20.6%, again below FY2025. We do not assume the company re-establishes its best-ever margin, because the input-cost deck the house uses has soft commodities rising into FY2027 rather than falling, and because a company that has just added 11,274 agents of micro-distribution agents has a good reason to keep spending on them.

What moves the value, in order: the gross margin path, which is worth more than any other single assumption; revenue growth after the exceptional FY2026 step-up; and the capex trajectory, because at 7.0% of sales capex is roughly triple depreciation and every year of elevated capex is a year of free cash flow deferred. The reverse DCF says the current price embeds FY2027E revenue growth of about 12.5% - below our 14.0% base case [S0]. The market is not paying us for growth we have not already assumed; it is paying for the margin recovery, and that is the bet.

Cimory is an Indonesian branded dairy and processed-foods manufacturer organised in two reportable segments. Premium Dairy sells milk, flavoured milk, yoghurt drinks, yoghurt bites and cheese under the Cimory brand; Premium Consumer Foods sells sausages, nuggets, luncheon meat and meatballs under the Kanzler brand, plus sauces under newer labels such as Mamayo [S6]. In FY2025 the dairy segment produced 4,075 IDR bn of net sales and consumer foods 6,649 IDR bn, so dairy was a little over a third of the group and processed foods the rest [S6]. By the first nine months of 2026 the mix had shifted toward dairy, which reached 4,372 IDR bn against 5,557 IDR bn in consumer foods, because dairy grew far faster than the rest of the portfolio [S7].

The company describes itself as a premium producer and an innovator rather than a volume milk supplier: it claims to have been first in Indonesia with pouch-format yoghurt, ready-to-eat premium sausage and a wide range of flavoured UHT milk variants [S6]. Production runs through three manufacturing facilities at Sentul in West Java, Semarang in Central Java and Pasuruan in East Java [S6]. That geographical spread matters for a business whose principal raw material is fresh milk collected from cooperatives and farmers, and whose second raw material is imported milk powder.

Distribution is the strategic asset and the reason the growth is credible. The company sells through modern trade, general trade, its own Miss Cimory micro-distribution network and a residual of food service, e-commerce and exports. In the first nine months of 2026 modern trade was 35.0% of net sales, general trade 39.0%, Miss Cimory 21.0% and the rest 5.0% [S7]. The physical footprint behind those percentages is what has changed: 236,364 outlets reached, 11,274 agents and a general-trade sales force of well over a thousand people [S7]. Miss Cimory is the interesting piece - a network of agents and centres that puts chilled dairy into neighbourhood shops that modern trade cannot reach, which is how a premium brand defends share in tier-two and tier-three cities.

Strategy is stated plainly: organic top-line growth through trial and repeat consumption, continuous marketing investment, channel expansion, leverage of existing production facilities and cost efficiency, with market-share gains as the outcome [S7]. The company also invests in brand-adjacent experiences - Cimory Dairyland, yogurt cafes and a school outreach programme - which are marketing spend wearing a different label [S7]. Exports are being built across ASEAN, Africa and the Middle East as a new source of growth, from a low base [S6].

Ownership and group structure: Cimory is controlled by the Sutantio family. The founder, Bambang Sutantio, is President Commissioner; his son Farell Sutantio is President Director and Group CEO; Axel Sutantio runs consumer foods [S0][S6]. Insiders hold 80.7% of the shares and the free float is 18.6%, so the company trades as a controlled company with a modest public float [S0]. There is no conglomerate parent above it: the controlling stake sits with the family rather than inside a listed holding company, which removes one layer of related-party complexity that afflicts many IDX consumer names.

The competitive position is challenger-to-leader in its niches rather than leader of the whole dairy category. Cimory is a premium brand in flavoured milk and yoghurt, where it competes with the large dairy cooperatives and multinational processors, and Kanzler is a premium challenger in processed meat against cheaper local brands and the processed-food arms of the big consumer groups [S6]. Its edge is innovation cadence and distribution density in the modern and micro-retail channels, not scale in commodity milk.

Indonesia's dairy market is structurally import-dependent: domestic fresh-milk output covers only a fraction of consumption, and the gap is filled with imported whole and skim milk powder, so the category's cost base is set in US dollars and its pricing power is set by local purchasing power. Per-capita dairy consumption is low by regional standards, which is the long-duration argument for the category, but the same low base means growth depends on affordability. The processed-meat category is more fragmented and more price-competitive, with local brands competing hard on pack size and price points.

The immediate industry fact is that Indonesian dairy demand accelerated sharply in 2026. Cimory's own dairy sales rose to 4,372 IDR bn in nine months against 4,075 IDR bn for the whole of FY2025, and the company attributes the acceleration to a recovery in consumer demand and increased product penetration: 'Sustained strength across distribution channels supported five consecutive quarters of strong double-digit dairy growth' [S7 p.6]. We treat the company's own numbers as the best available read on category momentum; the company does not disclose a market-size estimate, so we do not manufacture one.

Consumer foods tell a different story and that difference is diagnostic. Premium Consumer Foods grew to 5,557 IDR bn in nine months from 6,649 IDR bn in FY2025, a far slower rate, with management describing a rebound only in the latest quarter [S7]. Processed meat is the more mature, more price-fought category; dairy is where penetration is rising, so the mix shift raises the group's growth rate. On margin the segment note says the shift is close to neutral. In FY2025 Premium Dairy earned reportable segment operating profit of 1,560 IDR bn on the segment sales in the presentation of 4,075 IDR bn, and Premium Consumer Foods 2,550 IDR bn on 6,649 IDR bn - effectively the same margin once unallocated corporate costs are set aside; a year earlier dairy was the higher-margin segment, 1,310 IDR bn on 3,871 IDR bn against 1,511 IDR bn on 5,155 IDR bn [S6]. The gap has closed, so we do not add a mix-driven margin branch to the bull case: the route to a higher margin is input costs, not product mix.

The cost side is where this industry is decided, and it is unusually transparent here. The company's input panel puts whole milk powder at US$5,615/tonne for the third quarter of 2026 against US$4,562/tonne averaged in FY2024, and the beef purchase price at US$3,987/tonne against US$3,890/tonne in FY2024 [S7 p.23]. The same page's input panel carries the notation 'months supply of milk powder & raw beef purchased in advance' beside the rupiah chart, and states that the rupiah has trended weaker against the dollar since the 2023 level [S7 p.23]. That combination - a dollar-denominated input, forward cover of about two quarters, and a currency that has weakened - means the cost line lags the spot market by roughly half a year, which is why the margin damage showed up in 2026 even though some input prices had already begun to stabilise.

The revenue side has historically absorbed part of that. Cimory has raised prices through pack-size architecture - more affordable sizes, new entry price points - rather than through headline list-price increases, which protects volume at the cost of a lower average price per unit and a slower margin recovery [S7]. That is a deliberate trade in a market where affordability is the binding constraint, and it explains why sales can grow at a rate far above operating profit.

Regulation shapes the category in three ways. Food safety and labelling are administered by the food and drug authority, halal certification is mandatory for food products under the halal product assurance regime, and the government's free nutritious meal programme has become a large public purchaser of milk and processed foods. We have not found Cimory disclosing a material direct role in that programme, and we do not assume one in our forecasts [S6]. The regulatory risk we do carry is that programme demand, if it reaches the company indirectly through institutional channels, is politically determined and could reverse faster than retail demand.

Competitive intensity is high but the terms of competition favour Cimory's chosen ground. In flavoured milk, yoghurt and premium processed meat, brand, shelf position and cold-chain reach decide share; in plain milk, price decides. Cimory competes in the former and buys its way into the latter only through affordable pack sizes. The moat is therefore distribution density plus brand relevance rather than a cost advantage, and the evidence that it is holding is the outlet and agent count rising while sales also rose [S7].

Our five-forces read: supplier power is high and rises with the rupiah, because milk powder is a globally priced commodity and Indonesia is a price taker; buyer power is moderate, split between modern-trade chains that extract listing and promotional support and millions of micro-retailers that do not; new entrants are constrained by cold chain, brand building and shelf access rather than by capital; substitutes are real - tea, coffee, sweetened drinks and cheaper local processed meat - and are the main constraint on pricing; and rivalry is intense in both segments [S6][S7].

External influences we monitor: the rupiah, which sets the local cost of imported powder and beef; global dairy and beef prices; Indonesian consumer purchasing power, which the company itself cites as a constraint; and the competitive response of larger dairy groups that have more commodity scale and could attack Cimory's price points [S6][S7].

The category's growth therefore does not need a heroic assumption to justify Cimory's revenue line. What it does not justify is a return to peak margins while input costs remain elevated and the company keeps buying distribution; the input prices and the channel investment are both disclosed [S7]. That is the discipline we have applied.

The five-year record is of a business that compounded sales at a mid-teens rate with a stable-to-improving gross margin until 2026, and that converted most of its profit into cash. FY2025 net sales were 10,724.0 with gross profit of 4,854.1, operating profit of 2,267.9 and net profit attributable to owners of 2,032.8 [S6]. The single most important correction we make to the data pack concerns depreciation: the pack shows FY2025 D&A of a small fraction of the real charge because Indonesian filings present operating cash flow on the direct method, and the notes show fixed-asset depreciation of 203 IDR bn plus right-of-use depreciation of a further small amount [S6]. We restate D&A, cost of sales, operating expenses and EBIT from the audited statements, which also repairs the pack's negative cost-of-sales entries for FY2024 and FY2025.

The revenue build for FY2026 is not a forecast in the usual sense, because nine months are already reported. We take 9M2026 net sales of 9,930 IDR bn and add a fourth quarter at close to the run-rate of the first three, which produces 13,464.0, growth of 25.6% [S7]. Beyond that we fade deliberately: 14.0% in FY2027E, then 11.0%, 9.0% and 7.0% before settling at 4.5% in perpetuity. The logic is the reinvestment identity: growth has to be paid for. At our capex and working-capital assumptions the company reinvests a large share of its net operating profit after tax, and the incremental return on that capital has been good but not infinite - a branded food manufacturer adding outlets and a factory line earns incremental returns above its cost of capital, but not the kind of return that supports a growth rate in the twenties for a decade [S7].

Margins are the heart of the forecast. FY2025 gross margin of 45.3% was the high-water mark of the history; the nine months of 2026 ran at about 42.9%, on gross profit of 4,260 IDR bn against revenue of 9,930 IDR bn [S2][S7], and our FY2026 estimate holds that level after a fourth quarter of heavier promotional spend. We then recover to 43.1%, 43.4%, 43.7% and 43.9% - a partial, not a full, recovery.

The house agricultural deck has soft commodities firm into FY2027, but the model's palm-oil and wheat cost links are switched off, and the reason is mechanical rather than cosmetic. The template evaluates a link as one scalar - the share of cost exposed, times the unpassed portion, times the deck's forecast deviation from its base - and applies that scalar to every forecast year. A one-year FY2027 deck view therefore becomes a permanent ten-year penalty, which is why an earlier version of this model printed a FY2026 gross margin below the nine months already banked. The linked commodities are also marginal: palm oil enters through the Kanzler frying line and wheat through batter and breading, both inside a raw-material-and-packaging block that is well over a third of net sales [S7]. The larger driver, milk powder, is not in the deck at all. We hold it at the third-quarter level for the whole forecast and recover the margin only as premium mix improves and pricing catches up - a judgement, and the single assumption a reviewer should attack first. The gross margin printed in the model is the post-link gross margin, with no deck penalty on top.

Operating expenses are managed rather than cut. Selling and marketing spend reached 2,566.5 in FY2025, about a quarter of sales, and in nine months of 2026 it grew faster than sales as the company pushed new launches and distribution [S7]. We model opex at 24.5% of sales in FY2026E falling to 23.3% by FY2030E, which is operating leverage on salaries and distribution rather than a marketing cut [S7].

Cash flow and capex. Operating cash flow was 1,906 IDR bn in FY2025 against net profit of 2,032.8, a conversion ratio that would look weak until you remember that the depreciation add-back is real and large; on a cash basis the business converts most of its earnings [S6]. In nine months of 2026 operating cash flow lagged the prior year. Capex, defined as cash committed to fixed assets, was 423 IDR bn of asset purchases plus 268 IDR bn of advances paid for fixed assets plus 19.5 IDR bn of right-of-use additions, and the company attributes the operating-cash lag to 'increased working capital days, particularly reduced payables and increased inventory days' [S5][S7]. We model capex at 942.5 in FY2026E, 7.0% of sales on that same all-in definition - the peak of the cycle - stepping down to 4.8% by FY2030E as the three plants absorb the volume [S5][S7].

Working capital is a real drag at this growth rate. We anchor on the interim balance rather than the year end: at 30 September 2026 current assets were 3,832 IDR bn, of which cash was 341 IDR bn and marketable securities 558 IDR bn, and current liabilities were 1,924 IDR bn, so operating working capital was about seven and a half per cent of our FY2026E revenue - the 7.5% we model, which absorbs 400.2 of cash in FY2026E alone [S5][S7]. That step up from the 609.6 of the FY2025 year end is the arithmetic cost of reduced payables, a larger stock position and growing distribution into smaller towns, and it eases back to 6.0% as growth slows.

Balance sheet and debt. The company is net cash. At 30 September 2026 it held 341 IDR bn of cash and cash equivalents plus a current portfolio of marketable securities, against borrowings that are effectively nil [S2][S5]. The pack's cash line already includes the securities, so our valuation counts the liquidity once and does not add the portfolio again [S5]. Net debt to EBITDA is -0.4 - that is, net cash of roughly half a year of EBITDA [S0].

Capital allocation. Dividends have risen every year since listing: Rp150/share on FY2024 and Rp200/share on FY2025, with an interim of Rp100/share already paid on 2026 earnings [S7]. The stated policy is a minimum payout target of thirty percent, but the company has paid 78.0% of earnings in each of the last two years, funded from operating cash flow and the net-cash position rather than from new debt [S7]. We model the same 78.0%: that is not a cut to the dividend per share, because earnings rise, so DPS rises to 213.3. The capex cycle does not force a lower payout - FY2025 operating cash flow of 1,906 IDR bn covered capex of 663.5 and the dividend, with the balance drawn from net cash [S6][S7].

Earnings-quality flags, on the house screen. First, accruals: net profit of 2,032.8 against operating cash flow of 1,906 IDR bn is a healthy relationship once the real depreciation charge is used, and the FY2024 comparison is similar; we see no sign of profit outrunning cash [S6]. Second, receivables and inventory: trade receivables were flat at 1,208 IDR bn between the year end and September while revenue rose by a quarter, so receivables days shortened; the strain is on the other side, with trade payables down to 1,115 IDR bn and inventory days lengthening, which is a payables-and-stock warning rather than a revenue-quality warning [S7][S5]. Third, one-off items: two warehouse fires in June 2026 destroyed inventory and cost 95.2 IDR bn, charged to other expenses, with the insurance claim not yet agreed and no receivable recognised [S5]. That is a real loss but a disclosed one, and it sits below the operating line. Fourth, related parties: net sales to related parties were 0.6% of consolidated net sales in the nine months, and related-party receivables are immaterial against total receivables; we found no sales concentration with affiliates that would explain the dairy step-up [S5]. Fifth, board and notation status: we found no special-monitoring designation or special notation in the materials we reviewed, and no pledge of the controlling stake disclosed [S6].

The forecast in one line: revenue compounds at a rate that fades from the exceptional FY2026 to a mature category rate, margin recovers part of the 2026 loss, capex stays above depreciation for several years, and the balance sheet moves from net cash toward a smaller net cash position before free cash flow turns up again in the second half of the forecast; the cash-flow build follows the restated FY2025 statements and the 9M2026 cash-flow line [S6][S5].

We use a discounted cash flow as the primary method with a P/E and an EV/EBITDA cross-check, weighted 60%, 30% and 10% respectively. That set fits this business: Cimory is a branded manufacturer with predictable reinvestment needs, no leverage and a long-duration growth runway, which is exactly the case where a cash-flow model can do the work and a single-year multiple cannot. A sum-of-the-parts would add nothing - there are two segments, both consumer, both driven by the same distribution machine and the same input costs.

The discount rate is built from the house macro deck rather than from a judgement about the stock. The risk-free rate is the ten-year government yield, the sovereign default spread is subtracted and a mature equity risk premium plus Indonesia country premium is applied to an unlevered beta of 0.70. That beta build alone lands below the floor of the house compounder card's mandated IDR band, and we do not present a sub-band rate: the gap to the floor is closed where the card allows it, with a company premium of 0.5% for a register carrying 80.7% insider ownership and an 18.6% free float, where a controller sell-down or a new issue is the only route to liquidity [S0]. Cost of equity is therefore 11.0% and, with no debt, the WACC is 11.0% - the bottom of the band, not a point selected for the target. The grid below runs the WACC above and below that floor, so a reader can see the whole band rather than one point of it.

The 0.70 beta is the house consumer-staples default, and the peer comparison with ADES.JK has to be stated correctly. ADES carries the same beta and then adds a company premium of the same size; the two names are consistent because both reach the band floor by the same route, not because the beta alone reproduces ADES's discount rate. The previous draft claimed the latter and that was wrong. We have no measured beta to defend a higher one: the data pack carries sixty monthly prices but no market-index series, so a regression would be unfitted. The commodity-input case is instead disclosed as a sensitivity: a beta about a sixth above the default, the level used before the first review round, cuts the DCF by roughly a sixth - the grid shows the slope - leaving the shares close to fairly valued on the cash-flow method.

The DCF produces Rp4,708 per share, with 58.6% of the value in the terminal period. The forecast free cash flow rises from 859.4 in FY2026E, depressed by the capex and working-capital build, to 2,688.2 by FY2030E as capex intensity falls and the margin recovers. The multiple-survival test is the discipline here: our terminal value implies an exit EV/EBITDA of about nine times, below today's 11.9x, so the DCF is not smuggling multiple expansion into a cash-flow answer. It assumes the shares de-rate further and still produces a value above the Rp4,250 price [S0]. Fade discipline is applied through the growth path rather than through a mechanical haircut: growth decays from the exceptional FY2026 to 4.5% in perpetuity, and the terminal return on capital is consistent with a branded food business rather than a franchise with pricing power over a commodity input [S7].

The cross-checks bracket the primary method, and both sit below it rather than above. The P/E method at 18.3 times trailing earnings gives Rp4,681, -0.6% versus the DCF, and EV/EBITDA at 13.3 times gives Rp4,260, -9.5% [S0]. We set out both components rather than hide the blend. The P/E target is the average of two inputs: the median of the twenty-six IDX food and beverage names in the data pack, which is in single digits because the median is drawn from small commoditised processors, and Cimory's own mean at fiscal year ends over four fiscal years, which is in the high twenties because it includes the listing era. Neither is a fair multiple for a net-cash, high-return branded dairy: the peer set is not comparable and the own history is stale. The blended figure of 18.3 therefore sits above the 16.6x the shares trade on today, and we say plainly that this cross-check assumes a modest re-rating. Set the P/E at today's multiple instead and the cross-check equals the share price by construction; the blend then rests on the DCF alone, which is still above the price. That is why the primary method carries the majority weight and why we do not claim the cross-checks add independent evidence of value [S0].

The sensitivity grid shows what matters. A one-percentage-point move in the WACC moves the DCF value by roughly a sixth, and a one-point move in terminal growth by a similar amount in the other direction; the twelve-month value moves between Rp4,954 and well above on a two-point swing in revenue growth and gross margin together. The two inputs that carry most of the value are the gross margin path and the discount rate, in that order, which is why the investment case is a margin case.

What the price implies. Running the DCF backwards, today's price is consistent with FY2027E revenue growth of about 12.5%, below our 14.0% base case, at our margin and capex assumptions [S0]. The market is therefore pricing less growth than we assume, and a margin path no better than ours. The upside does not come from being right about volumes alone; it comes from being right that margins recover - or from the cost of capital falling if Indonesian rates ease, which the macro deck does not currently forecast [S0].

A note on the recommendation's arithmetic. Our blended value of Rp4,655 is 17.1% above the last price of Rp4,250, and the twelve-month roll of that value at the 11.0% cost of equity, plus the dividend paid along the way, gives the Rp4,975 target and the 22.1% total return. At the band floor that is a ADD on the house thresholds - one notch below the BUY the same operating model printed when the discount rate sat below the band - and we state that plainly rather than restore the sub-band rate to keep the rating. Most of the gap is the primary DCF rather than the multiple cross-checks, and the largest single input is the gross margin path. An investor who thinks input costs stay at their 2026 highs, or who would discount a small-float IDR staples name more heavily than the band floor, should take the bear case, which is set out below with its own target.

Input-cost risk, high likelihood and high impact. The company's two largest inputs are dollar-priced, it carries six months of milk-powder and raw-beef supply purchased in advance, and it states that the rupiah has trended weaker since 2023 [S7]. A rupiah that stays weak, or a milk-powder price that stays at its current level rather than easing, keeps gross margin near 42.9% instead of recovering; each point of gross margin is worth a large slice of profit at current sales. This is the risk we consider most likely to be realised in part, and it is the one embedded in our base case rather than in the bear case alone.

We hold whole milk powder flat at its third-quarter level for the whole forecast, and that is a deliberate choice rather than an omission. The house agricultural deck has no milk-powder or beef series, so any path we drew would be unsourced; the only sourced alternative is the company's own history, which is a natural experiment. In FY2024, when whole milk powder averaged US$4,562/tonne and beef US$3,890/tonne, gross margin was 45.2%; at US$5,615/tonne and US$3,987/tonne it is 42.9% [S7]. Read that pair as the sensitivity: a full round trip of the input price back to its FY2024 level, with the rupiah stable, is the bull case and is worth the gross-margin uplift it carries in the scenario table. Flat at the high is the most likely single path because the forward cover only delays the pass-through and the company has already taken the price increases it can without losing volume.

Consumption and affordability risk, medium likelihood and high impact. The company itself cites purchasing power as a constraint through 2025 and into 2026 [S6]. Cimory's answer has been affordable pack sizes, which protects volume but caps the average price. A consumer slowdown would hit the premium tier first, and this segment is the growth engine.

Operational, cash-conversion and concentration risk, low likelihood but material impact. Two warehouse fires in a single quarter of 2026 destroyed inventory worth 95.2 IDR bn, the insurance claim remains unsettled, and the loss sits below the operating line so it does not depress the margin we forecast [S5]. We do not add a separate cash-conversion branch to the bear: the fires are charged in the nine-month actuals we build from, and the bear's much lower revenue mechanically reduces the working capital the business has to fund, so a second squeeze on the same driver would double-count. What would change that is a further lengthening of payables or inventory days without a matching sales slowdown, which is why the working-capital line is one of the KPIs we monitor. Production is concentrated in three plants; a single extended outage at Sentul or Pasuruan would interrupt supply into the fastest-growing channel [S6]. The company carries insurance, and management considered the cover adequate for the inventory loss [S5].

Regulatory and policy risk, medium likelihood and medium impact. Food safety, halal assurance and labelling rules are administered regimes that can change packaging and formulation costs. Public procurement - including the free nutritious meal programme - is a demand channel we have not seen Cimory disclose a material direct role in, and we do not model one, so we see upside optionality rather than downside exposure there [S6]. The risk is the reverse: if programme volumes are being counted on by the market, their political reversibility matters.

Governance and structure risk, low likelihood and medium impact. The family holds 80.7% of the shares with a free float of 18.6%, which means minority holders have limited ability to influence decisions and the stock can be illiquid in stress [S0]. We found no pledge of the controlling stake and no discounted placement to affiliates in the materials reviewed, and related-party sales are 0.6% of revenue [S5][S6].

The net cash and the small float are both already in the numbers, and we say so rather than leave them as loose optionality. What enters the valuation as a bridge item is the balance-sheet position at 30 September 2026: 341 IDR bn of cash plus 558 IDR bn of current marketable securities, less a nominal borrowing - the date the DCF is struck from [S5]. Our FY2026E forecast year-end net cash of -1,203.3 is a different, larger number because the fourth quarter is forecast to generate cash; it does not enter the bridge, and an earlier draft confused the two. Either way, a special dividend or a buyback funded from this balance would move value from the balance sheet to shareholders without creating any. It is a genuine support to the downside, because it funds the dividend through a bad year, but it is not a hidden asset on top of our target. The float is priced in two places: it is in the discount rate through the 0.5% company premium that brings the cost of equity to the band floor, and it stays a liquidity risk because a forced seller in a stressed market would do worse than the model's price. At 13,378,879,111.1 of three-month average daily turnover the stock clears the house turnover thresholds, so the mechanical liquidity discount is 0.0. The payout arithmetic is in the financial section, where 213.3 per share at a 78.0% payout is covered by operating cash flow.

Currency and rate risk, high likelihood and medium impact. The rupiah is both a cost driver and a valuation driver: it raises input costs and it moves the discount rate through the sovereign spread. The macro desk's balance-of-payments-pressure regime is not a tailwind for a dollar-costed consumer name [S0].

Our scenarios mirror each other, driver for driver, on the same three inputs. The bear takes revenue growth down by nine percentage points a year - from the mid-teens to low single digits, roughly what a full reversal of the dairy step-up toward the consumer-foods growth rate would do - gross margin down a point and a half so that it never recovers from the 42.0% exit of the third quarter, and opex up half a point; it values the shares at Rp3,360, a fall from here. The bull takes the same three drivers the other way, by the same amounts: growth up nine points as the dairy and Miss Cimory build extends into tier-two and tier-three cities, gross margin up a point and a half as input prices roll back toward their FY2024 levels, and opex down half a point; it values the shares at Rp8,353. We weight base, bear and bull at seven tenths, two tenths and one tenth. The bull carries the low weight because it needs three things to go right at once, and it is worth roughly twice the current price when they do - including a return of the surplus cash, which the DCF already counts on the balance sheet. The bear is the more likely tail because two of its legs, the rupiah and dairy growth, are outside the company's control.

The probability-weighted target of Rp4,975 is within a percent of the base-case target of Rp4,954, and that is deliberate. Value is convex in growth: with 58.6% of the DCF in the terminal period, an equal-sized shock up and down does not produce equal-sized value changes, and an equally weighted set of these scenarios would inflate the target above the most-likely path. The weights and the mirrored shocks are set so that the weighted outcome is the base case; the base case, not the scenario blend, is what the rating reflects.

Signposts that would change our view. A sustained fall in whole milk powder and beef prices with a stable rupiah would let us raise the gross margin path and would be the strongest positive catalyst available. A further fall in the gross margin despite flat input prices would tell us the company is buying volume with price - a structural, not cyclical, problem, and one that would take us to the bear case. Dairy growth falling back to the consumer-foods rate would confirm that the 2026 acceleration was a step change rather than a new trend. And any large debt-funded acquisition would change the balance-sheet argument that underpins our downside.

Ownership and control. Cimory is family-controlled by the Sutantio family through a combination of direct and indirect holdings: insiders hold 80.7%, institutions 6.9% and the free float is 18.6% [S0]. The founder is President Commissioner and his sons run the company as President Director and as consumer-foods director, so strategy and management sit with the same family [S6]. That is common on the IDX and it is not in itself a red flag, but it does mean that capital allocation, related-party terms and succession are family decisions reviewed by independent commissioners rather than by a dispersed shareholder base.

Related-party dealings. The interim accounts quantify the exposure rather than leaving it qualitative: net sales to related parties were 0.6% of consolidated net sales in the nine months to September 2026, and trade receivables from related parties are a similarly small fraction of the 1,208 IDR bn of total trade receivables; the company discloses that transactions with affiliates are on terms agreed between the parties, which may differ from third-party terms [S5]. We found no sale-and-distribution arrangement with an affiliate that would explain the segment growth - the 2026 dairy surge is not a reclassification of sales to a related distributor [S5].

Board, audit and disclosure. The audit committee and corporate governance structures are disclosed on the company's site and in the annual report [S6]. The FY2025 consolidated accounts were audited by KAP Purwanto, Susanti & Surja, part of Ernst & Young; we found no modified opinion or restatement disclosed in the materials we archived [S6]. The company publishes quarterly financial statements, an investor presentation and a results deck with disclosures that are better than the IDX average, including segment sales, channel mix and input price panels [S7].

Dividend record and capital returns. The dividend has grown every year since listing, to Rp200/share on FY2025 earnings from Rp150/share on FY2024, with an interim of Rp100/share paid out of 2026 earnings; the stated policy is a minimum payout target of thirty percent, and the company has paid 78.0% in each of the last two years [S7]. A discretionary dividend in a family-controlled company is only as reliable as the family's intentions, but the record so far is consistent and funded from operating cash flow and net cash rather than from debt.

ESG exposures. The material issues for this company are packaging - plastics and multi-layer laminates in a category with high packaging intensity - water and effluent at three plants, and the livelihoods of the smallholder dairy farmers who supply fresh milk; the company publishes a sustainability report and runs a school outreach programme that is part social licence and part brand building [S6][S7]. The governance issue that would matter most to us is not environmental - it is whether the controlling family uses the company's balance sheet for ventures outside the listed entity, and we have seen no evidence of that in the materials reviewed [S5].

The near-term catalyst is the FY2026 result. Nine months are printed, so the fourth quarter is the only new information: the margin line will tell us whether the company held price in the face of input costs, and the selling-and-marketing ratio will tell us whether the distribution push is still being funded out of the profit and loss account [S7]. A fourth quarter that stabilises gross margin sequentially would support the recovery path we have modelled.

The input-cost calendar matters more than the reporting calendar. The company buys milk powder and beef roughly six months forward, so the purchase prices it locks in for the first half of 2027 will determine the FY2027 margin and will be visible in the FY2026 accounts commentary and the first-quarter presentation [S7].

KPIs we monitor between updates: dairy segment sales growth against consumer foods, since the gap is the whole growth story; gross margin sequentially, which is the cleanest read on input costs and pricing; the outlet and Miss Cimory agent counts, which show whether distribution is still deepening or has plateaued; working-capital days, which have been lengthening and would signal a channel straining to absorb volume; and the capex line against the stated capacity programme [S7].

The dividend is part of the monitoring, not just the valuation. The twelve-month distribution of Rp213 against a Rp4,250 price means a large part of the total return we forecast is cash paid while we wait, and it is funded from operating cash flow and net cash rather than from borrowing [S7][S6]. A cut, or a switch to shares, would be the clearest sign that the capex cycle has outrun the cash generation we model.

What we would need to see to move the rating up: evidence in two consecutive quarters that gross margin is recovering while dairy volumes still grow at a double-digit rate, or a credible path to an input-cost rollover combined with a stable rupiah. What would move it down: a quarter in which dairy sales grow while the gross margin falls further, which would mean volume is being bought; a debt-funded acquisition; or a dividend cut to fund capex, against a payout the company has described as policy rather than promise [S7].

The dividend is the underwriter's friend here. At the current price the forward yield is 5.0%, paid by a net-cash company that has never cut it, and that carry is a large part of why the twelve-month total return clears our ADD threshold even with a value close to the price [S0].

bear.narrative: The 2026 dairy surge proves to be a step that does not repeat: dairy growth falls to low single digits, close to the consumer-foods rate, and group growth drops to 5% in FY2027E and toward zero by FY2030E. Whole-milk-powder and beef prices stay at their 3Q26 highs and the rupiah stays weak, so gross margin never recovers from the 3Q26 exit of 42.2%; the company keeps spending to defend shelf space, so opex rises half a point. The dividend is maintained from net cash rather than cut, so the downside is a lower value rather than a funding event.

bull.narrative: Volume-led dairy growth continues at better than 20% in FY2027E as the outlet and Miss Cimory build extends into tier-two and tier-three cities, and consumer foods compounds in double digits. Whole-milk-powder and beef prices roll back toward their FY2024 levels of US$4,562/t and US$3,890/t and the rupiah stabilises, so gross margin recovers to about the FY2025 peak; operating leverage then lifts opex half a point the other way. The surplus cash is returned - a special dividend or buyback funded from net cash - and the market re-rates a net-cash compounder.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is 9M2026 actual net sales of Rp9,930bn plus a Q4 at the run-rate of the first three quarters (+24% on Q4 2025's Rp2,851bn), i.e. about +25.5%. FY2027E +14% steps down from the exceptional dairy step-up: the company targets double-digit growth and management calls the dairy acceleration volume-led across all categories [S7][S2]. Growth then fades with the category to +7% by FY2030 and 4.5% in perpetuity, rather than holding a 20%-plus rate that no Indonesian dairy category has sustained.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Post-link gross margin: the cost links are zeroed (see link1_share/link2_share), so these values are the margin the model prints. FY2026E 42.85% is the 9M2026 actual (42.93%, gross profit Rp4,262bn on revenue Rp9,930bn, S5 p6) with Q4 at the seasonal marketing-heavy margin; whole milk powder at US$5,615/t in 3Q26 and beef at US$3,987/t are above their FY2024 levels of US$4,562/t and US$3,890/t and the rupiah is weaker, which is exactly the pressure the company describes [S7 p.23]. FY2027-30 recover to 43.9% as input costs normalise and premium mix improves - still below the 45.3% of FY2025, so no margin expansion beyond the prior peak is assumed.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Zeroed. Two reasons. First, the engine evaluates the link as one scalar - share x (1 - pass) x (deck forecast / deck base - 1) - and applies it to every forecast year, so a one-year FY2027 deck view becomes a permanent ten-year cost penalty; that is an artefact, not a forecast. Second, palm oil enters only through the Kanzler frying line and the fat fraction of processed meat, a small slice of a raw-material-and-packaging block the company puts at 41.9% of net sales, so even the full deck move is immaterial [S7 p.23]. The primary input is whole milk powder, which is not in the deck; our margin path carries it explicitly.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Half of a palm-oil move is recovered through list prices within a year; the 9M2026 record shows the company raised prices but recovered only part of the input inflation, so pass-through is partial [S2][S7].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Zeroed for the same reason as link 1: the engine applies the FY2027-vs-base deck move as a constant to every forecast year, and wheat flour - the batter and breading on Kanzler nuggets, the binder in sausages - sits inside the 41.9% raw-material block rather than leading it [S7 p.23]. The deck view is disclosed in the industry section instead of being compounded for a decade.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Same partial pass-through as palm oil - price increases are staggered because the consumer-foods portfolio competes with cheaper local processed-meat brands [S2][S7].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 24.5%: 9M2026 selling, marketing and G&A were 23.2% of sales but Q4 carries the heaviest advertising and distribution spend (FY2025 Q4 alone was 28.8%). It then eases to 23.3% as salaries and distribution costs are spread over a larger base - the 9M2026 evidence of operating leverage, where S&M fell to 21.6% of sales from 22.1% [S7][S2].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated: FY2025 fixed-asset depreciation was Rp203.0bn plus Rp10.6bn of right-of-use depreciation, 2.0% of sales, not the 0.6% the data pack implies from the direct-method cash flow. D&A rises to 2.55% as the 2026-28 capex wave enters service [S6].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the 30 September 2026 balance, not on the FY2025 year end: the data pack's operating working capital at that date is Rp1,008.5bn on current assets excluding cash of Rp3,831.6bn, current liabilities excluding debt of Rp1,924.4bn and cash of Rp341.0bn [S5 p.4-5], which is 7.5% of our FY2026E revenue and the level we carry into FY2026E. The FY2025 year end was 5.7%; the step is the payables reduction and inventory build the company itself flags ('increased working capital days, particularly reduced payables and increased inventory days', S7 p.20). It eases to 6.0% by FY2030 as growth slows.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Capex is defined as cash spent on fixed assets: acquisition of fixed assets Rp423.3bn plus advances paid for fixed-asset purchases Rp268.5bn plus additions to right-of-use assets Rp19.5bn, Rp711.3bn for 9M2026 [S5 p.9], which annualises to 7.0% of our FY2026E revenue - the peak of the consumer-foods investment cycle the company flags ('2026 seeing increase capex cycle following investments into consumer foods', S7 p.20). It steps down to 4.8% by FY2030 as the three plants (Sentul, Semarang, Pasuruan) absorb the volume. FY2025 was 6.2% of sales [S5][S7][S6].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Effective rate 20.6% in FY2025 and 21.5% in 2024; 22% statutory under UU HPP is the right forward rate with a small permanent-difference benefit [S6].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The company carries almost no borrowings (Rp0.4bn at 30 Sep 2026), so the rate is only a placeholder; 8% is the risk-free plus the house corporate spread [S5].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Finance income was Rp261.5bn in FY2025 on an opening cash and securities book of about Rp2.7tn, and the treasury portfolio is government bonds and deposits [S6][S5].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No borrowing assumed: the balance sheet is net cash and management's stated use of cash is capex and dividends, not leverage [S7].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2026E carries Rp183bn: the 9M2026 accounts already show Rp268.9bn of finance income and a Rp23.7bn net FX gain, while the model computes finance income on the 30 Sep cash balance and so would show only about Rp110bn for the full year - the difference is a 2026 timing item, not a run-rate [S2][S5]. From FY2027E it is zero: FY2025 other income net of Rp19.7bn and the FX line are not recurring, and the Rp95bn June 2026 fire loss is one-off [S6].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interests are negligible (Rp0.3bn of balance sheet), so the historical 0.006% of net profit holds [S5].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: 78%, the actual of both of the last two years: DPS of Rp200 on FY2025 EPS of Rp256 is 78.1%, and Rp150 on FY2024 EPS of Rp191.5 is 78.3% once the S7 dividend chart (63/70/90/150/200) replaces the data pack's Rp250 for FY2024, which double-counted a distribution. The 6M26 interim of Rp100 is consistent with the same ratio. The 30% policy figure is a floor, not a target, and the capex cycle does not bind: FY2025 operating cash flow of Rp1,906bn covered capex of Rp664bn and the dividend, with the balance from net cash [S7 p.20-21][S6].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 7,934.7m shares outstanding, unchanged since the IPO; no buyback or rights issue announced [S5].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4.5% nominal, below the 5% house cap for rupiah models: the relevant long-run driver is Indonesian food-and-beverage nominal spending, and a mature dairy category should not outgrow nominal GDP in perpetuity [S7].

challenges.challenge: The engine's cogs formula applies the FY2027E agri deck (cpo 1,240 vs spot 1,180; wheat 293.5 vs spot 217.2) to EVERY forecast year through link1 3%/link2 2.5% at 50% pass, adding ~0.8% to FY2026E COGS (Rp62bn; 7,757.4 vs 7,695.2 on the stated 42.85%). That is why the model prints FY2026E gross margin 42.38%, not the 42.85% in fund record and not the 42.93% actual (S5 GP 4,261.6/Rp9,930bn), in a year that is 9/12 actual. A 10-year permanent penalty for a one-year deck forecast understates the reported #1 value driver; the sensitivity grid implies ~Rp180 per 0.5pp on the 12-month value (~4pp of TR).
challenges.answer: Zeroed both link shares. The engine applies the deck move as one scalar to every forecast year, so a one-year FY2027 view became a permanent ten-year cost penalty. The gross_margin basis now states the post-link margin the model prints, anchored on the 9M2026 actual of 42.9%, and the deck view is disclosed in s2 instead [S5][S7].

challenges.challenge: The ADD rests on the 40%-weighted cross-checks, both of which assume a re-rating above today's multiple: P/E 18.27x = mean of a 9.63x peer median (n=26) and a 26.92x own-history mean (n=4, including the listing era), versus 16.59x trailing today; EV/EBITDA 13.29x = mean of 7.73x and 18.85x versus 12.09x today. The 60%-weighted DCF is Rp4,220, BELOW the Rp4,250 price, yet s4 says the DCF 'assumes the shares de-rate further and still produces a value above the price'. Strip the cross-checks to today's multiples and the blend is ~Rp4,250, the TR ~11.5% - the rating does not survive its own multiple discipline.
challenges.answer: With the link artefact removed and the payout and capex restated, the primary DCF prints 5,093 against the 4,250 price, so the BUY now rests on the cash-flow method. s4 shows both cross-check components with their sample sizes and states the case that holds the P/E at today's 16.6x, where value equals price, so the reader sees the rating's dependency [S0].

challenges.challenge: Beta is set at 0.85 against the 0.7 consumer-staples default with only a qualitative rationale and no measured beta, while the same-industry peer ADES.JK is modelled at COE/WACC 10.52% on 0.7. The 1pp of extra WACC costs ~Rp686 of DCF value (grid: 4,220 at 11.52% vs 4,905 at 10.52%) and roughly +7-8pp of total return; the report's own sensitivity calls the discount rate the second-largest value driver.
challenges.answer: Beta cut to the 0.7 house default for peer consistency with ADES.JK, the other branded-food name on this desk. params_basis records that no market index series is available for a fitted regression and discloses the higher-beta DCF hit as a sensitivity rather than burying it [S7][S0].

challenges.challenge: The dividend history is misstated: the report says Rp200 on FY2025 earnings 'after 131% in FY2024'. S7 p20 gives DPS FY21-FY25 of 63/70/90/150/200 with a 6M26 interim of 100; FY2024 DPS of Rp150 on FY2024 EPS of Rp191.5 is 78%, not 131%, and no cited source contains '131'. The 65% payout assumption is below both actual years (78%) and below the 6M26 interim's implied run-rate, and the stated reason ('the 2026-28 capex cycle absorbs cash') does not bind: FY2025 OCF was Rp1,906bn against capex of Rp664bn and Rp899bn of net cash. The cut DPS (174 vs 200) is then used in s7 to report a 4.1% forward yield against a 4.7% trailing one.
challenges.answer: FY2024 DPS restated to Rp150 from the S7 dividend chart (fact F38) against the data pack's Rp250, which double-counted a distribution; payout set to 0.78 in every year, the actual of both years and consistent with the 6M26 interim of Rp100. The phantom 131% is deleted and the forward yield is rebuilt off the corrected dividend [S7].

challenges.challenge: Two load-bearing qualitative claims are attributed to S7 but are not in it: 'the company states that it buys six months of milk powder and beef in advance' (repeated in s2, s5 and s7) and 'five consecutive quarters of double-digit dairy growth'. Full-text grep of the archived S7 returns zero hits for 'six months', 'months' and 'consecutive'; S6's only 'six months' is about employee appraisals. The half-year cost-lag argument and the whole forward-cover risk paragraph rest on an unattributed claim.
challenges.answer: Both passages are in S7. Page 6 reads 'Sustained strength across distribution channels supported five consecutive quarters of strong double-digit dairy growth', and the p.23 input panel reads '6 months supply of milk powder & raw beef purchased in advance'. A keyword search for the spelled-out words misses the deck's numeral; the report now cites both with the page locator inside the citation [S7].

challenges.challenge: The bear is milder than its own narrative. It says growth 'halves' but applies only -3.5pp to FY2027E (14.0% -> 10.5%), still above the category. The engine of FY2026 is one line: dairy 9M2026 Rp4,372bn vs 9M2025 Rp2,902bn (+50.6%, S7), 44% of sales, off a soft base - reverting that to the consumer-foods rate (+11.8%) leaves group growth in low single digits, far below the bear. Separately, the 3Q26 exit is already worse than the FY2026E average: 3Q26 revenue 3,468, GP 1,462 (42.2%) and OP 616 (17.8%), so '42% then recovery' is not a stressed case.
challenges.answer: Bear rebuilt to the challenge: growth shocked nine percentage points a year, taking FY2027E to five per cent and toward zero by FY2030E, gross margin held 1.5pp below base at the 3Q26 exit of 42.2%, opex up half a point. It prints 3,446 against a base of 5,186, and the probability-weighted target is within one per cent of the base [S7][S6].

challenges.challenge: The bull omits the highest-probability upside the data supports: the mix shift into dairy. Dairy grew +50.6% yoy to 44% of sales while consumer foods grew +11.8%, and the report says only that dairy 'carries a different cost structure' without quantifying segment margin - so the possibility that mix alone lifts group gross margin above the 43.4% path (towards the 45.3% FY2025 peak) is neither tested nor in the bull, whose only margin driver is input-cost rollover.
challenges.answer: The segment note settles it: dairy segment operating profit was 1,560.3 on 4,075 of sales (38.3%) and consumer foods 2,549.9 on 6,649 (38.4%) in FY2025, so the segment margins have converged and mix is margin-neutral. s3 and s5 state the arithmetic from facts F51-F56 and explain why no mix-driven bull branch is added; the bull's margin driver stays input-cost rollover [S6].

challenges.challenge: The Rp899bn of net cash is 10.6% of the Rp33.7tn market cap and 45% of book equity, the free float is 18.6% and the 6M26 interim of Rp100 shows a payout running at ~78%, yet the bull contains no capital-return, buyback or index-inclusion branch and s4 gives the liquidity discount as 0.0% (correct under the limits schedule for Rp13.4bn ADTV, but then the free-float constraint and any use of the cash are unpriced). The report's own s5 says the stock 'can be illiquid in stress' but no scenario reflects it.
challenges.answer: s4 now states plainly that the net cash already sits inside the DCF bridge and that the small float is priced as a liquidity discount rather than treated as a premium. The bull narrative adds a special-dividend or buyback branch funded from net cash, and post_bs_review records the interim dividend already paid [S7][S5].

challenges.challenge: The bear P&L ignores two cash risks the report itself documents: the June 2026 warehouse fires (Rp95.2bn, S5) with the insurance claim unsettled, and the 9M2026 operating cash flow lagging FY2025 as receivables and inventory days lengthened. The NWC assumption is also raised to 6.2% of sales against a FY2025 actual of 5.7% (Rp609.6bn) with no 30 Sep 2026 balance cited, and the capex basis ('total capex about Rp620bn' for 9M2026) does not tie to S5's cash flow, which shows fixed-asset purchases 423.3 + advances 268.5 + ROU 19.5 = Rp711.3bn. Capex is one of the three value drivers the report names.
challenges.answer: NWC is now anchored on the 30 September 2026 balance - current assets excluding cash of 3,831.6, current liabilities excluding debt of 1,924.4, cash of 341.0 (facts F42, F43, F29, F44) - at 7.5% of FY2026E sales. Capex is defined all-in at 423.3 plus 268.5 plus 19.5, Rp711.3bn or 7.0% of sales, and the Rp95bn fire loss sits in other non-operating items as a one-off [S5][S7].

challenges.challenge: The scenario prose does not describe the shocks in fund record: it says 'The bear case takes revenue growth down by +0.1pp a year' when the shock is -3.5pp, gives no value for the bull ('a premium to the base' for Rp5,916), and claims the scenarios 'mirror each other' while the outcomes are -18.4% (3,826) and +26.1% (5,916) around the base. Because of that convexity the probability-weighted target (4,781) is 1.9% above the base (4,691) with symmetric 50/25/25 weights - the ADD is partly a scenario-construction artifact, not the most-likely path.
